story_type: controlled demolition of collapsed bridge wreckage lying on a cargo ship's bow
hook: Part of a collapsed bridge lay across this ship. So they blew it off.
narration: Salvors set off charges on a piece of the Key Bridge lying across a cargo ship's bow.
Since March twenty sixth, two thousand twenty four, that section of the collapsed bridge had rested on the bow of the ship Dali.
Ship and steel sat in the Federal Channel, the way in and out of the Port of Baltimore.
Precision cutting uses small charges placed right on the steel, slicing it at chosen points so the wreck falls away in pieces.
On May thirteenth, section four dropped off the bow and into the river.
outcome: A week later the Dali was moved, and after about fifty thousand tons of wreckage came out, the channel was certified safe on June tenth.
title: Blasting a fallen bridge off a ship
description:
Salvors with the Key Bridge Response Unified Command use precision cutting charges on section 4 of the collapsed Francis Scott Key Bridge, which rested on the bow of the M/V Dali in Baltimore, Maryland, on May 13, 2024.

Footage: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers video, via DVIDS: https://www.dvidshub.net/video/923331/unified-command-performs-controlled-demolition-precision-cutting

extra_sources.excerpt: Since March 26, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and U.S. Navy Supervisor of Salvage and Diving worked to clear Key Bridge wreckage and move the M/V Dali from the Federal Channel.

The Unified Command safely moved the M/V Dali on May 20 and widened the Limited Access Channel to 400 feet May 21, permitting all pre-collapse, deep-draft commercial vessels to transit through the Port of Baltimore.
Fully restoring the Federal Channel to its original width and depth involved the removal of about 50,000 tons of bridge wreckage from the Patapsco River.
Following the removal of wreckage at the 50-foot mud-line, the Unified Command performed a survey of the Federal Channel June 10, certifying the riverbed as safe for transit.
